Compiled by the Junior Disciple Venerable Weigai Zhu while Residing at Cui Feng Chan Monastery on Mount Dongting,

The morning sun emerges, clearing away the misty clouds; The thirsty find broth, the cold find firewood.
Awakening to the transformation of retribution, one knows it is not real; One proceeds toward peace and security, shaking off the dust of the world.
Wang Shusheng extensively propagated the Buddha’s work; He shattered the six heterodox schools, responding with a mere snap of the fingers.
The Dharma came from the East; it was not a meeting at a boundary. The robe of faith was transmitted; with a single sandal, he departed.
He honored the Five Mountains as true vessels of the Dharma. He stood amidst accumulated snow, his extraordinary arm enduring both the patient and the impatient.
Having attained the marrow of the Dharma, the debt must surely be repaid; there shall be descendants.
Mount Huankong lies hidden; the Buddha-sun is obscured. Flying southward on my travels, I stand like a fallen tree.
I beg for liberation; how powerful is wisdom! It drives away the stinging bees and wasps.
The Divine Mountain guards Poutou Peak; the multitudes of clouds follow. It spans the six qi and distills the two lineages.

Teaching according to one's inclination, Leisurely and relaxed, The child of Huangmei, A youth upon the road— Lacking the seven marks [of a Buddha], Yet realizing all things as empty. The Sage serves with diligence, A laborer at the pestle and mortar.
Verse on Harmonizing the Mind: Striking down the clashing peaks, Rushing southward through the night, I encounter this in my heart.
The Emperor bowed his head, seeking instruction from beneath the Master’s wind. The boat was renewed; the leaves returned to the thicket.
Those who possess the Way attain it through non-action. The world has its succession; the fourfold assembly relies on him as a lamp.
The transmission continues like the resonance of the *xun* and *chi* flutes. The Master’s singular endowment began from the time he was a mere child.
Jin Zhenjun ascends the ladder of the sages; His compassion is firm and pure. Unable to offer [worldly] service, he gives rise to reverence and filial piety;
In the end, he wears coarse hempen mourning. Xian shaves his hair and becomes a monk;
Ying seeks clarification, traveling east of the Han River. He plucks out the blindness and deafness [of ignorance]; He clears away the overgrown weeds and wasteland.
Formerly there was nothing; now all is vast and winding. Meeting with drenching moisture, sprouts and shoots emerge.
The frogs croak; the bells have not yet been struck. The scales of fish hide; the bright pearl is revealed.
Two towering mountains gather beneath the eaves. From ten thousand miles away they come; their feet are calloused from the long journey.
The thunder roars in spring, opening the burrows of the hibernating insects; it distinguishes bondage from liberation and decides where to go and where to stay.
It pours forth clarified butter and ladles out nectar. One hundred and fifty generations have filled the roads with their chariots;
they recite the words and phrases, gazing upon the skeletal eyes, as the scrolls are painted upon silk.
Far away are Hu and Yue; nearby are staff and sandals. Casting off coarse appearances, all attain awakening.
The mountain paths are dense and overgrown; the springs murmur in deep seclusion. Tiger tracks crisscross; wildcats and monkeys screech.
The gate of the stupa is closed; pine and cypress branches entwine. The heavens hang low in the south; the sea glimmers with light.
Tattered robes and worn-out garments; a single mat for bedding. They come to circle about, prostrating their five limbs before me.
Their bodies are strong, yet their sustenance fills only their throats. Habituated to resentment and hatred, they find sweetness in putrid fish and dried meat.
They gaze askance at the True Vehicle as if it were a superfluous tumor. I rejoice in my birth, able to distinguish the fragrance of the incense from the stench of the rancid.
I long to offer encouragement and guidance, yet it seems utterly beyond reach. I shall carve this upon a hard stone to dispel my sorrow.
The fifth day of the second month in the second year of the Zhiping era, the year of Yisi (1065).
